opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the core reason is that there's a huge gap between how mathematicians write proofs and what a computer actually needs in order to check them.

When a mathematician writes a proof on paper, it's really a compressed argument meant for another trained human. We skip steps all the time. We say "it's easy to see," or "by a standard argument," or "without loss of generality," and the reader fills in the details from shared experience and intuition. A paper proof might be ten pages, but the actual logical content, written out fully, could be hundreds or thousands of steps.

Lean doesn't share any of that intuition. Every single step has to be justified from definitions and previously proven results. So the first big cost is just unpacking all those implicit steps. Things that feel completely obvious, like some inequality holding or two ways of describing an object being the same, can take a surprisingly long time to formalize.

The second issue is infrastructure. Lean has a big community library called Mathlib, and it's grown enormously, but it still doesn't cover everything. If your proof relies on some piece of theory that hasn't been formalized yet, you have to build that foundation yourself before you can even start on your actual result. That's often where most of the time goes. You set out to prove one theorem and end up formalizing half a textbook first.

Third, there's the matter of choosing the right definitions. On paper you can switch between equivalent viewpoints freely. In Lean, the way you set up a definition determines how easy or painful everything downstream becomes. A bad choice early on can make later proofs extremely awkward, and refactoring is expensive. Getting the design right takes experience, almost like software engineering.

And finally, there's simply a skills gap. To be productive you need to be both a good mathematician and fluent in the proof assistant: its tactics, its type theory, the conventions of the library. Not many people have both yet, so even experts move fairly slowly compared to writing on paper.

That said, I think this is changing quickly. The library keeps growing, the tooling keeps improving, and AI systems are starting to help with the tedious low-level steps. So the cost is high today, but I don't think it will stay this high for long.

r001.rationale: The response says that when Mathlib lacks theory a proof depends on, the formalizer must build that foundation before proving the result, which can take most of the time.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think the biggest reason is that a Lean proof and a paper proof are two very different artifacts, even when they prove the same theorem. When I write a proof on paper, I'm writing for another mathematician. I can say "by a standard compactness argument" or "the rest follows similarly," and the reader fills in the gap. Lean doesn't fill in gaps. Every one of those "obviously" steps has to be spelled out, and sometimes a sentence in a paper expands into hundreds of lines of code.

The second thing is the library. Mathlib is enormous now, but it's still nowhere near covering all of modern mathematics. So when you formalize a real result, you often discover that some lemma you assumed was "known" simply isn't there, and you have to go build it, and the thing it depends on, and so on. A lot of the time isn't spent on the theorem you care about. It's spent on infrastructure.

And then there's the mismatch between how mathematicians think about objects and how they're actually defined in the library. A paper might treat a function as living on the real numbers, but in Lean it might be defined on a subtype, or there's a coercion somewhere, and you spend hours convincing the system that two things that are "obviously the same" actually are the same. People call this the definitional-equality problem, or just "fighting the elaborator," and it's a huge time sink for beginners especially.

The last piece is that there aren't that many people who are both strong mathematicians and comfortable with the tooling. The community is growing fast, and tools like automation and now language models are starting to help with the tedious parts, but today it's still largely a craft. So when people ask why a proof that fits on two pages took a team months, the answer is usually all of those things stacking on top of each other.

r001.rationale: The response says that needed lemmas may be absent from Mathlib and must be built along with their dependencies, making infrastructure work a significant time cost.

astra-6.text:
I think the main reason is that the level of detail a mathematician needs is very different from the level a computer needs. When we write a proof, we might say, “It’s obvious that…” or “By a standard argument…” A reader can fill in those gaps. In Lean, those steps still have to be justified, either explicitly or through automation.

So a proof that takes half a page on paper can involve a lot of work. You have to choose how to represent the objects, find the relevant results in the library, and make sure their assumptions match what you have. Sometimes the mathematical idea is clear, but connecting all those pieces is time-consuming.

There’s also the work of building the foundations. If a result you need hasn’t been formalized yet, you may have to formalize it first. But that work is reusable. Once the supporting theory and automation are in place, later proofs can become much easier. So the time isn’t just spent translating a particular proof; some of it goes into building the infrastructure for future proofs.

r001.rationale: The response says that when a needed result has not yet been formalized, it may have to be formalized first, and notes the work of finding results in the library. This communicates the time cost of formalizing missing dependencies.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main reason is that the level of detail a computer needs is very different from what a mathematician needs. When we write a proof for another person, we skip a lot of steps. We might say, “It’s obvious,” or “By a standard argument,” because we trust the reader to fill in the gaps. In Lean, those gaps have to be filled, either explicitly or through automation.

You also have to build on the right definitions and existing results. Sometimes the mathematical idea is quite simple, but expressing it in a form that fits the library takes a lot of work. You may have two objects that a person considers essentially the same, while Lean needs you to explain precisely how they are related.

So the time isn’t necessarily spent finding the central argument. A lot of it goes into making all the surrounding assumptions and connections explicit. As the libraries and automation improve, that work becomes easier to reuse.

r001.rationale: The response says that fitting definitions and results to the library takes work, but it does not attribute the time to mathematical dependencies missing from Lean’s library.
